content.p: The Commisso clan is one of the best-known families of the 'Ndrangheta, the mafia of Calabria. Its home is Siderno, a town on the Ionian coast, but Italian and Canadian investigators have for decades described it as a transatlantic organisation, with relatives and associates in Ontario and, more recently, in the state of New York. Canadian police call the cluster of Siderno clans in their country "the Siderno Group", a label that appears in Canadian court proceedings going back to the 1970s, according to an Italian prosecutor.

The record is uneven. Some members have been convicted in Canada. The best-known, Cosimo Commisso, served 26 years in an Italian prison over five murders before an Italian court acquitted him on review in 2019; the country's highest court confirmed that outcome in January 2020. Many of the other names that appear in the press have only been accused or named as suspects, and several deny any link to organised crime.

An Italian prosecutor, Giuseppe Lombardo, has said that the Siderno group's reach beyond its home territory was already evident in 1975, at the time of the killing of Antonio Macrì. The clan's overseas story is usually dated to 1961, when three brothers, Rocco Remo, Cosimo and Michele Commisso, arrived in Canada, according to a recap of the Netflix series Mafia: Most Wanted. The same recap says Rocco Remo survived two shooting attempts during trips back to Siderno in 1971 and 1972.

The recap credits a former associate with the clan's first big trouble in Canada. Cecil Kirby, born in Toronto in 1950, worked for the clan from 1975, it says. In 1980 he secretly approached the RCMP and, wearing a wire, gathered evidence that the recap says led to convictions of the Commisso brothers, among others. Of those, only one is independently confirmed: the Post reports that Rocco Remo Commisso was convicted in 1981 on three counts of conspiring to commit murder, and again in 1984 over his part in a bombing that killed one person. The recap adds that, after testifying, Kirby went into witness protection and, according to it, the 'Ndrangheta allegedly put a six-figure bounty on his life.
content.h2: The Siderno murder case against Cosimo Commisso
content.p: In Italy, Cosimo Commisso faced a separate case. He was arrested in January 1993 on charges of leading a mafia clan and of masterminding five murders. The Toronto Sun reported that he was sentenced to life in 1998 for five murders and three attempted murders committed between May 1989 and July 1991, a series of killings the press called the "Feud of Siderno". The paper put his time behind bars at 26 years.

In January 2019, the Toronto Sun reported, a review before the Court of Appeal of Naples ended in his acquittal, on the ground that he had not committed the offences. A year later, on a Wednesday in January 2020, Italy's Court of Cassation confirmed that the review appeal had been valid and threw out an appeal by the Naples prosecutor general. The Sun, citing the Gazzetta del Sud, wrote that the court ruled Commisso had no hand in the settling of accounts. The Sun added that he stayed in custody on other matters and that "local sources" said he remained at the top of the 'Ndrangheta. That was a claim by the newspaper's sources, not a finding of a court.

Canada has also sent clan figures back. The Globe and Mail noted in 2010 that in 2005 Antonio Commisso, described as a high-ranking capo, was arrested and returned to Italy after fleeing to Woodbridge to escape a conviction for mafia association. In 2008 Giuseppe Coluccio was deported from Toronto to face a similar charge. The OCCRP reported that Antonio Coluccio, whom Canadian immigration authorities had linked to the Commisso clan, was refused landed immigrant status, deported in 2008 and later arrested in Italy in 2014. OCCRP reported that he was found guilty of corruption and sentenced to 30 years. According to the same report, wiretaps between Canadian and Italian 'Ndrangheta members were used as evidence against him and others.

In December 2010 Italian prosecutors named seven Ontario men in warrants that came in a sweep that produced 53 arrests. Among those named was Francesco Commisso, then 62, who was not arrested. Another named man, Salvatore Oliveti, a businessman, denied through his lawyer any link to the mafia. The Globe and Mail explained a legal gap that frustrated the Italian side: simply belonging to the mafia is an offence in Italy but not in Canada. Prosecutor Nicola Gratteri called Canada "an important hideout" for fugitives and said Italian authorities had identified nine clan-based groups, or locali, operating in Ontario. He said Italian authorities wanted more cooperation from the RCMP.

In September 2015 a large Italian investigation named, according to the National Post, more than a dozen current or former residents of Canada. Gratteri said it involved "the richest" 'Ndrangheta families and said the clans around Siderno had earlier been found to have 500 gunmen ready to take up arms. The Post reported that prosecutors named the Commisso, Aquino-Coluccio and Crupi clans as the focus. It also reported that Rocco Remo Commisso, who has been named for decades as part of the mob in Canada, was among those named. Those arrested had not yet had a chance to answer the accusations, the paper noted.

On 29 June 2018 a man and a woman were shot dead on a residential street in Woodbridge, north of Toronto. York Regional Police gave the names of the dead as Cosimo Commisso, aged 33, from Vaughan, and Chantelle Almeida, aged 26, from Toronto. The National Post wrote that the man shared a name and family ties with a man long reputed to be a Toronto mafia leader. It said police sources described him as not a known criminal but as having personal associations with crime figures. The paper added that his family owned a Woodbridge restaurant and bar that had been shot at the previous September, a case that had not been solved, and that investigators believed he was an associate of John Ignagni, who was killed in a Toronto parking garage in 2016. Police declined to say whether organised crime played any role. The newspaper's reporting does not say who killed the pair.

In July 2019, Italian operation "Canadian 'Ndrangheta Connection", which produced 12 arrests in Italy, gave investigators what the National Post called a surprising picture of power. For decades, the Siderno clans in Canada, about seven of them, had been run by a board called the "camera di controllo", subordinate to the mother clans in Calabria under a body known as "il Crimine di Siderno". Police in both countries said the board north of Toronto could now take decisions affecting not just Canada but also Siderno itself, an arrangement investigators described as a "criminal blockchain". Anna Sergi, a University of Essex criminologist, said that wiretaps appeared to show the Toronto board extending its reach to Siderno "for the first time reversing the order". An Italian police official, Fausto Lamparelli, called the concentration of authority in Canada unprecedented. These are the allegations of Italian investigators.

In February 2026 Reggio Calabria's anti-mafia prosecutors and the Carabinieri's ROS unit, with FBI support, announced Operation Risiko against what they called the Siderno branch of the Commisso clan. Corriere della Calabria reported that seven people were accused of mafia association, damage and extortion aggravated by the mafia method, and that the shares of a construction firm were seized. The prosecutor's detention order was not validated by the preliminary-investigations judge in Locri, but the judge issued an order of custody in prison for all of the suspects. ReggioToday noted that all of them must be considered presumed innocent until a final verdict.

Corriere della Calabria said the investigation ran from 2019 to 2025, within a longer effort that Lombardo put at nearly two decades (ReggioToday reported nearly 15 years, starting in early 2008), in cooperation with the FBI that investigators called prolonged and fruitful. He described a unitary structure rather than separate cells: in Italy, according to investigators, the clan was led by Antonio Commisso, born in 1980, who is presumed innocent and who took the lead after his father Francesco went into hiding in Canada and an uncle was jailed. A lower unit, the "ndrina di contrada Mirto", operated locally. At the centre of the case was Frank Albanese of Albany, New York, described by prosecutors as the head of the clan's American arm, who allegedly linked Siderno to groups abroad, supported fugitives in Canada and travelled to Italy several times between 2019 and 2025. Lombardo said the prosecution had mapped the activity of the 'Ndrangheta in the state of New York and the continuing presence of Commisso representatives in the Ontario area, and that Canada's earlier "Phoenix" judgment gave formal recognition of the organisation's presence there. A Siderno councillor, Carlo Fuda, who was not under investigation, resigned after wiretaps allegedly showed him asking Antonio Commisso to pressure a creditor in return for cleaning Antonio Commisso's private roads with municipal vehicles.
